evidence: Cic. Inv. 2.54.164: continentia est, per quam cupiditās cōnsiliī gubernātiōne regitur (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Self-control within: Lewis & Short calls it “the common signification”, most frequent in Cicero, and sets it against abstinentia, which looks to the outward thing one keeps one’s hands off. Temperantia is the same virtue named as moderation.

terms.gloss: self-restraint toward what is not one’s own; integrity
evidence: Cic. Off. 2.22: conciliāre benevolentiam multitūdinis abstinentiā et continentiā (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: it “always has reference to the outward object from which one restrains himself”, above all other people’s property, so it is the honest official’s virtue (abstinentiā et continentiā, Cic. Off. 2.22); later it is also fasting.

terms.gloss: in possession of oneself, in one’s right mind
terms.grammar: adjective compos, compotis, with the genitive
terms.comment: In Livy minds estranged by discord are made compotēs suī again, brought back to their senses: it is being master of oneself, not the virtue of restraint (see sane).

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
